content.content:
1	# Committing and pushing
2	
3	**scratch**
4	: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.
5	
6	Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.
7	
8	## What to commit
9	
10	- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
11	- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
12	- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
13	- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
14	- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
15	- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.
16	- Name a model by its tier (Opus, Sonnet, Fable) in any text that you commit, commit messages included. Never write its model identifier, the API's name for the model, which starts with `claude-`.
17	
18	## How to commit
19	
20	Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:
21	
22	    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>
23	
24	- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
25	- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
26	- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
27	- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
28	- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
29	- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:
30	
31	      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
32	      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB
33	
34	  If your brief gives another session line, use it. If a commit that is already made has a footer that names a model, by any name or identifier, leave the commit as it is. Such a footer is not a defect: do not check for it, report it or list it.
35	
36	## Pushing
37	
38	Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.
39	
40	- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
41	- From a session in a cloud container, do not try to delete a branch on GitHub, or retry a refusal with another tool (the `cloud-container` skill, "Rules for every agent"). Removing a worktree does not delete its branch, which stays. Ask nobody in your report to delete a branch.
42	- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
43	  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
44	  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
45	  3. If it lists only your commits, push the three refs with this one command, and wait for it to end:
46	
47	         git push --atomic origin main main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8 main:blinded-fable
48	
49	     With `--atomic`, the three refs update together or not at all. Do not pipe the command into another command, since a pipe hides a refusal. A refusal shows as a line that starts with `!`, and as a non-zero exit. The last ref keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
50	- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
51	- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and do not run it again. Report the refused ref and git's message.
52

1	<!-- The specification as HTML for a phone, in two editions since 2026-11-15: `spec2html.py` converts `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (the team's Working Draft of February 2011) into the static reader under `docs/specification/`, which GitHub Pages serves at https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/, and `Specification/` (the LaTeX that the revival revises) into `docs/specification/revival/`, whose pages ask not to be indexed; `editions.html` lists the specification at its milestones; LaTeX itself sets every example, displayed formula, table, grammar box and drawing, and dvisvgm turns them into SVG whose text is text; the reader keeps the place, notes along the text and their export in the browser; this note says how to run the converter and its three checks, what the curator decided, and what differs from the PDF. -->
2	
3	# The specification as HTML for a phone
4	
5	`spec2html.py` converts the specification's LaTeX into a reader of static pages: the front matter, the 43 chapters and the 10 appendices, 54 pages. GitHub Pages serves them once `main` is pushed (`.github/workflows/pages.yml` publishes `docs/`). Nothing comes from another site.
6	
7	## The two editions
8	
9	The curator's decision of 2026-11-15: the team's text has the public address, and the revival's edition steps back, out of the search engines. `--source` names the source root, and the source root names the edition.
10	
11	| | The Working Draft of 2 February 2011 | The revised edition of the 2026 revival |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| `--source` | `Specification-1.0-frozen` | `Specification` (the default) |
14	| Pages | `docs/specification/`, https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/specification/ | `docs/specification/revival/` |
15	| Beside the LaTeX, the conversion reads | the team's tree at the draft's commit `2f8b4331a` (F-163): `SpecData/`, `Fortify/`, the `.fsi` files of the library, taken from git into the work folder | the working tree |
16	| Work folder | `/tmp/spec-html-work-draft` | `/tmp/spec-html-work` |
17	| The revival's layer (callouts, tint, legend, "archived copy" links) | none | as before |
18	| `<meta name="robots" content="noindex">` | on no page | on every page |
19	| What the edition adds, and where | the reader's controls; the lines that start "This edition:" in small monospace (class `edline`): one under the title of the contents, one over each library listing, one in the front matter, and the foot of each page | one line at the top of each page (class `edline top`): "The Fortress revival's revised edition of 2026, not the text of the Fortress team", with a link to the same page of the Working Draft |
20	| Storage in the browser | `fortress-spec.*`, the keys in use since the first sample | `fortress-spec-revival.*` |
21	
22	- **The pointer at the foot of a Working Draft page** links to the same chapter of the revised edition and says one of three things. "Changed this chapter": the chapter's LaTeX differs under the two roots (the chapter's own text and every file that it reads, comments apart; `chapter_latex`); 28 pages. "Did not change the text of this chapter; … its examples or library listings are those of the tree of 2026": the LaTeX is the same, and an example, a table of reserved words or a listed `.fsi` file differs (`chapter_companions`); 2 pages, the two chapters of library listings. "Did not change this chapter": 24 pages.
23	- **`editions.html`**, written by the build of the Working Draft and linked from the contents page of both editions, lists 1.0α, 1.0β, 1.0, the Working Draft and, set apart under "Not the team's work", the revised edition. Its dates and facts are from `Specification-history/README.md`, `explorations/coordinator/spec-editions-leads-2026-11-10.md`, F-163, `pdfinfo` and git. The build copies the three PDFs into `docs/specification/pdf/` (2.4, 2.0 and 1.2 MB; the same blobs as in the tree, so the repository does not grow). The PDF of the revised edition (2.5 MB) is linked at its GitHub address, not served from the site. The tree holds no PDF build of the Working Draft of 2011.
24	- **`revised-only.js`**, written by the build of the Working Draft from the pages of the revised edition: for each chapter, the ids of the blocks that only the revised edition has. Both editions load it (see "The notes across the two editions").
25	- **Build order.** The revised edition first, then the Working Draft, which reads the revised pages for `revised-only.js`. A crawler's `robots.txt` cannot be served for this site from this repository (it is read at the host's root only), so the `noindex` tag is the measure; `check.js` checks it on every page of both editions.
26	- **The examples of the Working Draft** are set as the team's tree of February 2011 set them: its `foreg` writes the `Fortress` environment, where the later tree's writes `FortressCode`. The converter takes both.
27	
28	A first sample of 2026-11-10 held the front matter and chapters 1 to 6. The curator read it and decided how the rest is made; `curator-notes.md` holds his words. This run follows them:
29	
30	1. Examples and displays are LaTeX converted to SVG. The converter's own rendering of displayed code and formulas is gone.
31	2. Code words and formulas inside a sentence stay HTML text, with the three rules of `reader.css` that he approved (no ligatures in code, the inline highlight with narrow side padding, serif curly quotation marks). Those rules are unchanged.
32	3. Every table and display is compared with the PDF. "The checks" below says how, and what a person still has to look at.
33	4. An address of the authors' text gets the edition's link to the Internet Archive.
34	5. The revival's paragraph in the preface has the tint of the revival's additions, and the opening explains the tint.
35	6. A quote pair around the whole of a typewriter span is curly; an apostrophe inside code stays as typed.
36	7. Where the specification shows ASCII, the page shows ASCII.
37	
38	## The files
39	
40	- `spec2html.py`: the conversion and the site's pages. Python 3 with its standard library and `fontTools` (to read the fonts it makes). It runs `latex`, `dvisvgm` and Emacs (for the tree's Fortify).
41	- `reader.css`, `reader.js`: the reader. The build copies them into `docs/specification/`.
42	- `check.js`: the reader in Chromium at a phone's width (below).
43	- `compare.js`: every display in Chromium against LaTeX's own picture of it (below).
44	- `pdfcheck.py`: the words of every block against the words of a PDF (below).
45	- `notes-export-2026-11-15.txt`: the curator's 15 notes as he exported them before the editions were parted; `check.js` imports them.
46	- `curator-notes.md`: the curator's decisions and notes.
47	
48	The build also writes `tex-fonts.css` and `fonts/` in each edition's folder: the fonts of the displays.
49	
50	## Running it
51	
52	From the repository root:
53	
54	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --list            # every chapter with its slug
55	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --try variables,functions
56	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --try all
57	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py                   # the revised edition, into docs/specification/revival/
58	    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/spec2html.py --source Specification-1.0-frozen   # the Working Draft, into docs/specification/
59	
60	`--source` goes with every form above (`--list`, `--try`).
61	
62	- A plain run takes about a minute when the work folder is warm, and about three minutes when it is empty. It rewrites every page of its edition's folder: the 54 chapter pages, `index.html` (the contents), `notes.html`, `references.html`, `reader.css`, `reader.js`, `tex-fonts.css` and `fonts/`. No page is edited by hand.
63	- `--try` converts into the work folder only (`<work>/try/`, with the reader's files, so the pages can be opened) and prints, for each chapter, what did not convert. It writes nothing under `docs/`.
64	- `--chapters a,b` publishes only those chapters; a cross-reference into a chapter that is left out shows its number and "[not converted yet]".
65	- The script exits 1 if a published chapter holds a construct that it did not convert, a display on which LaTeX reported an error, or a display that uses a character that the fonts lack. Such a place shows in the page in red, and the report names it.
66	- `--work` sets the scratch folder (by default one for each edition, see the table): the examples as Fortify renders them, the LaTeX file of each chapter's displays with its log, the SVGs, the fonts. `--base` sets the public address that the links of exported notes start with.
67	- For the revised edition the script reads `Specification/`, `SpecData/examples/`, `SpecData/tables/`, `Fortify/`, and the `.fsi` files of `Library/` and `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`; for the Working Draft it reads `Specification-1.0-frozen/` and the same folders as `git archive 2f8b4331a` gives them. It writes nothing in the original tree. It builds and runs no Fortress.
68	
69	## How the text is converted
70	
71	The script is a converter of its own over the macros that the chapters use (`pandoc` and `htlatex` were tried on the first sample: the first drops Fortify's markup without a word, the second stops under the tree's macros).
72	
73	- **Structure.** It walks the `\input`s from `Specification/fortress/fortress.tex` and numbers parts, chapters, sections, subsections, figures, lemmas and theorems as LaTeX does. Each page is one chapter. A section's anchor is its label (`\seclabel{overview:apis}` gives `#sec-overview-apis`); a section without a label gets `#s-` and its title.
74	- **Running text** becomes HTML: paragraphs, lists, headings, footnotes, the authors' `\note` boxes ("Draft note"), the revival's `\revision` callouts. Fortify's markup and formulas inside a sentence become HTML text with Unicode characters, italics, superscripts and subscripts. The `\newcommand`s of `Specification/latex-common/macros/` are read and expanded, and so are the definitions that a chapter makes for itself (`\def`, `\newcommand`, `\renewcommand`, `\RenewDocumentCommand`), and the macro files that Appendix A reads for each of its calculi, in its order.
75	- **Displays** are set by LaTeX. A display is an example (`\begin{Fortress}`, or a file of `SpecData/examples/` that the tree's tool `foreg` renders, as the specification's `ant genSource` does), a displayed formula (`\[ \]`, `$$ $$`, `align`, `eqnarray`), a table (`tabular`, `array`), a grammar box (`Grammar`, `GrammarTwo`), a `tabbing` or `ttt` block, a drawing (`*.eepic`), and a table of reserved words (written as the build's Perl scripts write it). For each chapter the script writes one LaTeX file with the preamble of `fortress.tex` and one page for each display, in a box of the PDF's text width; the chapter's own definitions go into the file at their places; the labels of the whole specification go into its `.aux` file, so that a reference inside a display prints its number and links to its page. `latex` sets the file, `dvisvgm` converts each page, and the script puts the SVG into the page, inline.
76	  - The text of a display is SVG text in the TeX fonts, so it can be selected and copied. The fonts are made by dvisvgm from the fonts of the TeX installation and are served from `fonts/`; a page loads only those that it shows.
77	  - One SVG serves the light and the dark theme: its ink is `currentColor`, the colour of the text around it.
78	  - A display wider than the screen scrolls sideways inside its frame, at the PDF's proportions: a display is not reflowed.
79	  - A footnote inside a display joins the chapter's footnotes, and the display shows its number.
80	  - An example that has a source form shows it too, as before: the lines between `(** EXAMPLE **)` and `(** END EXAMPLE **)` of the `.fss` file, or the commented lines that the authors left before `\begin{Fortress}`. A switch above an example changes all examples.
81	- **A formula inside a sentence that HTML text cannot show** (an array, an overstruck operator, a binomial, a command that the converter does not know) is set by LaTeX too, as an SVG on the line's baseline. There are 83 of them, most in chapters 16 and 34 and Appendix A. Every other inline formula is HTML text, as the curator decided.
82	- **The API listings of the library** (chapters 29 and 30) are made as the build makes them: the tree's tool `fortex` on a copy of each `.fsi` file. Their code is set by LaTeX, their documentation comments are running text. They show the library as it is in the tree today.
83	- **Cross-references** are links. **Citations** show the key of the work and link to `references.html`.
84	
85	## The edition's layer over the authors' text
86	
87	This layer is the revised edition's only; the Working Draft has none of it. The source text is not changed for any of this; the converter adds it, and it is visible as the edition's.
88	
89	- **The tint.** What the 2026 revival added stands on a light tint of the ground (`.rv` and `aside.revision` in `reader.css`, the colour `--rev-bg`, in light and in dark): the callout of a revised passage, the revival's paragraph in the preface, the revival's section of Appendix I, and the links below. The contents page and the preface open with one sentence that shows the tint and says what it means. The converter knows the revival's paragraph and section from two short lists at its top, `REVIVAL_PARAGRAPHS` and `REVIVAL_SECTIONS`: the source does not mark them.
90	- **Archived copies.** Beside each address of the authors' text (`http://projectfortress.sun.com` and the others, also in the references), the edition puts a link "archived copy" to `https://web.archive.org/web/2008/<address>`. The Internet Archive resolves a partial date to the nearest capture. 2008 is the year of the release that the preface names with the address; `ARCHIVE` at the top of the script sets it. The container cannot reach the Internet Archive, so no link was opened.
91	- Not built, because the curator has not decided it: marking which words of a revised passage changed (`curator-notes.md`, "The revival's callouts do not show which text changed").
92	
93	## The reader
94	
95	- **Place.** A chapter page stores, in `localStorage` under `fortress-spec.place.v1` (the Working Draft) or `fortress-spec-revival.place.v1` (the revised edition), the block at the top of the screen, for each chapter and for the last one read. The start page offers to continue there; a chapter opened from the contents offers the place where that chapter was left.
96	- **Notes.** The pencil at the end of a paragraph, in the bar of a code example, under a table or beside a heading opens a text box under that place. `notes.html` lists all notes, exports them as text, and imports such a text. They are kept under `fortress-spec.notes.v1`, or `fortress-spec-revival.notes.v1` in the revised edition.
97	- **Without storage** (private browsing) the pages work, a note lasts until the page is left, and a warning says so.
98	- **Select.** The button beside a heading selects that section's text up to its first subsection, for Speak.
99	
100	### The ids that notes hang on
101	
102	- The id of a paragraph is a hash of its words (`#p-934d16e7`). Every paragraph of the first sample keeps its id, among them the two that carry the curator's notes, `preface.html#p-0ea553b6` and `preface.html#p-033235cb`. To keep them, the hash still counts the words "[not converted yet]" after a reference into a chapter outside the first sample, as that sample showed them; the edition's own links are not counted.
103	- One paragraph of chapter 4 changed its id, because its words changed: the one with a quote pair inside a typewriter span (decision 6). 
104	- The ids of tables (`t-`), grammar boxes (`g-`), and code blocks without a source form (`c-`) changed: 34 in the first sample's chapters (14 in chapter 2, 12 in chapter 4, 2 in chapter 5, 6 in chapter 6). They were hashes of the HTML that the converter's own rendering made, which is gone; they are now hashes of the display's LaTeX source. A code block with a source form keeps its id. `reader.js` keeps a note whose place is gone and lists it at the top of its chapter, with the words it was written on.
105	
106	### The notes across the two editions
107	
108	Notes written before 2026-11-15 were written on the revised edition at the addresses that now show the Working Draft, and they are in the browser under `fortress-spec.notes.v1`. `localStorage` belongs to the host, not to the folder, so both editions can read it.
109	
110	- The Working Draft keeps that key. A paragraph that the revival did not change has the same words, so the same id, in both editions, and its note stays on it.
111	- A note on a block that only the revised edition has (its id is in `revised-only.js`) stays in the Working Draft's storage. Its chapter page lists it at the top with "The passage of this note is in the revised edition" and a link to the passage there; `notes.html` lists it with the same words, and the export gives it the link into `revival/` and a line `Edition: the passage of this note is in the revised edition`. An import reads such a note back.
112	- The revised edition has its own storage. Once, on the first page of it that a browser opens, it takes a copy of the notes of the old key whose passage only it has, so that such a note also shows on its passage; nothing else is copied, and nothing is removed from the old key (`fortress-spec-revival.adopted.v1` records that it was done).
113	- Of the curator's 15 notes of `notes-export-2026-11-15.txt`, 14 stay on their paragraphs of the Working Draft (`preface.html`: `p-0ea553b6`, `p-f85a28b6`, `p-0ee6a8b8`, `p-56c0c623`, `p-3e0c2dfb`; `intro.html`: `p-f9d62312`, `p-284c2aab`, `p-edfaffe1`, `p-a3cd883e`; `overview.html`: `p-136580aa`, `p-18267c77`, `p-ade874e1`, `p-e17a0706`, `p-ffe59943`), and one, on the revival's paragraph of the preface (`p-033235cb`), is listed as a note whose passage is in the revised edition and is copied there. `check.js` imports the file and checks this.
114	
115	## Changes to reader.css and reader.js
116	
117	Of 2026-11-15, for the two editions:
118	
119	- `reader.js`: the storage keys take their prefix from `data-store` on `<body>` (a page without the attribute has `fortress-spec`, as before); `data-edition` on `<body>` is `draft` or `revised`; `window.FORTRESS_REVISED_ONLY`, if a page defines it before `reader.js`, marks the notes whose passage is in the revised edition (their link, a line on their card, a line `Edition:` in the export), and lets the revised edition take its copy once. A page that sets none of the three behaves as before.
120	- `reader.css`, added at its end: `.edline`, `.edline.top` (the edition's own lines), `ol.editions` and `section.apart` (the page of the editions). No rule was changed or removed.
121	
122	Of 2026-11-13:
123	
124	For a page that uses the reader's files, such as the walk-through under `docs/microgpt/`:
125	
126	- `reader.js` is unchanged.
127	- No rule of `reader.css` was changed or removed, and no class was renamed.
128	- Added to `reader.css`, at its end: `svg.tx` and `svg.tx.il` (a display, and one inside a sentence), `.mw` (the frame of a long formula inside a sentence), `.rv`, `a.ed`, `.legend` (the edition's layer), `.doc` (the documentation text of an API listing), `.hr` (a rule inside a formula), and `white-space: normal` for `.m` inside headings, `dt`, `figcaption`, `summary` and `nav`.
129	- The converter no longer writes these, whose rules stay in the stylesheet: `.fx-r .tb`, `.fx-r .l`, `.gapline`, `.cm`, `table.tab`, `table.grammar`, `div.words`, `.tw.gr .label`. `.fx-r`, `.dm` and `.tw` now hold one `svg.tx`.
130	- A chapter page with displays links `tex-fonts.css` and carries a `<style>` with the font classes of its SVGs (`svg.tx text.t0` and so on).
131	
132	## The checks
133	
134	Serve the pages, then run the three:
135	
136	    mkdir -p /tmp/spec-srv && ln -sfn "$PWD/docs" /tmp/spec-srv/fortress
137	    python3 -m http.server 8765 --directory /tmp/spec-srv &
138	    S=explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html U=http://localhost:8765/fortress/specification/
139	    node $S/check.js $U                                   # the Working Draft
140	    node $S/check.js ${U}revival/ /tmp/shots-revised      # the revised edition
141	    node $S/compare.js /tmp/spec-html-work-draft $U
142	    node $S/compare.js /tmp/spec-html-work ${U}revival/
143	    python3 $S/pdfcheck.py                                # the revised edition against Specification/fortress.pdf
144	    git show 414b790e3f:Specification/fortress.pdf > /tmp/spec-html-work-draft/draft-2026-08-21.pdf
145	    python3 $S/pdfcheck.py --pages docs/specification --pdf /tmp/spec-html-work-draft/draft-2026-08-21.pdf
146	
147	The tree holds no PDF of the Working Draft. The nearest is in git: `414b790e3f` (2026-08-21) committed the first PDF that the revival built, before it revised the text; its LaTeX differs from the frozen copy in the preamble of `fortress.tex` (the build's repair) and one line of `basic-lib/objects.tex`, and its library listings are those of the library of that day. `pdfcheck.py` on the Working Draft runs against that file.
148	
149	- **`check.js`** (about a minute) opens every page that the contents lists at 390 px, light and dark. It fails on a page that scrolls sideways, on a construct left unconverted, on a display whose font is missing or lacks a character, and if the ink of the displays is not the colour of the text in both themes. It reads the edition from the page and checks: in the revised edition, `noindex` on every page, the line at the top with its link to the same page of the Working Draft, the two note-carrying ids of the preface, the archive link and the tint; in the Working Draft, no robots tag, no callout, tint, legend or archive link on any page, the link to the revised chapter at the foot and nowhere else, and the curator's 15 notes of 2026-11-15 across the two editions. In both it checks that the text of a display can be selected, the three rules for code inside a sentence, and the curly quote pair. Then, as before: notes on a paragraph, a code example and a heading, the place, export and import, the switch between the two forms of the code, Select, that no request leaves the site, and the pages without `localStorage`. It saves two screenshots.
150	- **`compare.js`** (about five minutes) sets each chapter's displays a second time, with `pdflatex` from the same file, makes a picture of each page with `pdftoppm`, takes a picture of the same display in Chromium, and compares the two: their sizes, and the share of the ink of each that lies within two pixels of the other's. This is the check that would have caught the chapter 4 tables of the first sample. It found two faults while this run was built: dvisvgm wrote the Courier font without the characters U+002E to U+005F when it wrote the whole font at once (the fonts are now written in pieces of 32 codes, and the build reads each piece back and fails if a character that a display uses is missing), and the frame of a table lost its top and left lines at the edge of the picture (each SVG now has a margin).
151	- **`pdfcheck.py`** (ten seconds) reduces every paragraph, heading, list item, caption and display of the pages to its letters and digits, does the same with the text of `Specification/fortress.pdf`, and looks for each block's runs of ten characters in the PDF. A block that lost a row, was set from the wrong source or was filled with something else fails. It found the lemma numbers of Appendix B, the lost footnotes of grammar boxes, and four commands that the text form had mishandled (`\rule`, `\vspace*`, `\not` before a macro, and the calculi's own `\exp`).
152	
153	Results of 2026-11-15, on both editions:
154	
155	- `check.js`: all pass on the Working Draft (45 checks) and on the revised edition (42).
156	- `pdfcheck.py`, the revised edition: 6,845 blocks, 8 not found, as on 2026-11-13. The Working Draft against the PDF of `414b790e3f`: 5,680 blocks, 18 not found: 7 displays of chapter 29, whose listing is the library of February 2011 where that PDF lists the library of August 2026, and 11 blocks at 58–75 % of their runs, dense with symbols or holding a draft note.
157	- `compare.js` (about fifteen minutes for each edition when both run at once): the Working Draft, 1,177 displays compared, 3 differ; the revised edition, 1,229 compared, 4 differ; none by a fault of the page. The three of chapter 16 are those of 2026-11-13, in both editions. The fourth, display 1 of chapter 26 in the revised edition, holds a reference: the second LaTeX run frames it as hyperref frames a link, which makes its picture seven pixels wider.
158	
159	Results of 2026-11-13, on the 54 pages (then one edition, the revised one):
160	
161	- `check.js`: all pass.
162	- `compare.js`: 1,229 displays compared, 5 differ, none by a fault of the page. Three of chapter 16 agree to 77–92 % where the limit is 92 % (one small glyph, and a row of typewriter symbols that the two renderers hint differently). One of chapter 23 holds a citation and one of chapter 33 a reference, which the reader shows as a key and a link and the second LaTeX run shows as `?`.
163	- `pdfcheck.py`: 6,845 blocks compared, 8 not found in the PDF, each with 63–75 % of its runs where the limit is 75 %: three paragraphs and five displays dense with symbols (chapters 9, 13, 16, 40 and Appendix F), read and found right. 98 more are displays of symbols with too few letters to judge by words; `compare.js` covers them.
164	
165	What these checks do not do, and what was looked at by eye:
166	
167	- No tool here places a display beside its page of the PDF. `compare.js` compares with LaTeX's picture from the same source and macros as the PDF, and `pdfcheck.py` compares words with the PDF. Together they cover every display, but neither is a person looking at the PDF's page.
168	- Looked at beside the PDF's page, at 390 px and at a desktop's width: the preface; the character tables of chapter 4 (page 45 of the PDF, the curator's example: the `&`, the row, and the white brackets are right) and its reserved words (page 51); the grammar boxes of sections 7.1 and 9.5 (page 96); Figure 16.1 (page 172); Figure 22.1 (page 228); the first two figures of Appendix A (page 506); sections F.2 to F.4 of Appendix F (page 547).
169	- Not looked at beside the PDF by a person: the other displays and tables, among them most of the 979 rows of the operator tables of Appendix F, the inference rules of Appendix A apart from the first figure, and the API listings.
170	
171	## What differs from the PDF
172	
173	| What | Where | Why |
174	|---|---|---|
175	| A display does not reflow | every chapter | It is LaTeX's page at the PDF's width; on a phone a wide one scrolls inside its frame. |
176	| Formulas inside a sentence are HTML text in the device's fonts | every chapter | The curator's decision. Brackets do not stretch, spacing is the browser's, a fraction is two short lines. |
177	| Some symbols of a display copy as private-use characters | displays with `⟦ ⟧`, `⊢`, primes, large delimiters and other glyphs that the TeX fonts name without a Unicode value | dvisvgm gives such a glyph a code point from U+E000. The picture is right; a copy of the text, and Speak, get a character without meaning. |
178	| The bibliography's numbers | every `\cite`, also inside displays | The PDF numbers the cited works; the reader cites by key, `[JLS]`, and `references.html` lists every entry of `fortress.bib` under its key. |
179	| The index | every `\index` | Dropped; the reader has no index page. |
180	| The arrowheads of the five drawings are solid | chapter 22 | The PDF is made by pdflatex with `eepicemu`, which cannot fill; the reader's drawings come from `latex` with `eepic`, which fills them as the drawing asks. |
181	| Figures and tables stay where their source is | every chapter | None floats to the top of a page. |
182	| A display inside a draft note has the size of the text | a few notes | In the PDF the note's box sets it smaller, in the sans face. |
183	| The API listings show today's library | chapters 29 and 30 | They are made from the `.fsi` files of the tree, as the build makes them; a listing has no source form in the reader. |
184	| The page numbers of `\pageref` | rare | The reader has no pages. |
185	| The title page and the table of contents | front | The contents page of the reader stands for both. |
186	| Appendix I's section of the revival is tinted as a whole | Appendix I | The edition's layer. |
187	
188	The commented source before a hand-written example is the authors' own, and nothing checks that it still matches the LaTeX under it.
189	
190	## Faults of the source text that the conversion met
191	
192	Nothing under `Specification/` was changed. These are for whoever edits it:
193	
194	- `Specification/basic-lib/objects.tex:17` holds `\tracingcommands=1\tracingmacros=1`, a TeX debugging switch left in the chapter. It prints nothing, but it makes the build's log very large from there on.
195	- `Specification/basic/expressions/literals.tex:45`, in a margin note: ``\b'' is LaTeX's accent command (a bar under the next character), where the authors meant a backslash and the letter b. The PDF shows a quotation mark with a bar under it.
196	- `Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:866`: of three quoted code points in one sentence, the second has its quote pair inside the typewriter span and the others outside (`` `\txt{001C}', \txt{`FBAB'}, `\txt{1D11E}' ``). The reader shows all three alike.
197

        \txt{OMEGA} & \emph{becomes} & $\Omega$ &
        \txt{omega} & \emph{becomes} & $\omega$
\end{tabular}

A restricted word that is not a short name specified by Fortress
is compared to names of characters
specified by the Unicode Standard~\cite{Unicode}.
Because restricted words consist only of
letters, digits and underscores,
while Unicode names may include hyphens and spaces
(but not underscores),
hyphens and spaces in the Unicode names
are replaced by underscores for this comparison.
Specifically,
if a restricted word is the official \unicode\ name of a character
with hyphens and spaces replaced by underscores,
it is replaced by that character.
For any Unicode character other than the control characters,
there is a unique official \unicode\ name
not shared by any other Unicode character.
Since control characters are protected,
they do not present a problem in this regard.

If there is no matching official \unicode\ name,
the restricted word is compared to the alternative names for characters
specified by the Unicode Standard,
again with hyphens and spaces replaced by underscores,
and converted to a character with such a matching name.
If more than one character has a matching alternative name,
then the restricted word is converted to the first such non-protected character
(i.e., the one with the smallest code point).
If there is no matching alternative name,
then the restricted word is compared to
official \unicode\ names
and any alternative names specified in the Unicode Standard,
with underscores in place of hyphens and spaces,
where any of the following substrings may be omitted:
\begin{verbatim}
  "LETTER_"
  "DIGIT_"
  "RADICAL_"
  "NUMERAL_"
\end{verbatim}
If there are multiple such substrings in a given name,
any combination of them may be omitted.
Again,
if there are multiple characters with matching abridged names,
the restricted word is converted to the first such non-protected character.

If the restricted word is not converted to a single Unicode character
by any of the above rules,
parts of it may be converted as follows:
If the restricted word begins with the short name
(i.e., the name in the table above)
of a Greek letter followed by an underscore or a digit,
or ends with the short name of a Greek letter
that is preceded by an underscore,
or contains the short name of a Greek letter
with an underscore on each side of it,
then the short name of the Greek letter
is replaced by the Greek letter itself.
In the same manner,
the character sequence ``micro'' is replaced
with the character \txt{MICRO SIGN} $\mu$
(U+00B5,
which looks just like the Greek lowercase mu $\mu$ but is different).
If a word-part being thus replaced
has an underscore to each side,
and the underscore on the right is the last character of the restricted word,
then the underscore on the left is removed as the name is replaced;
this ad hoc rule is for
the sake of the abbreviations of certain dimensional units,
so that, for example, \txt{micro\_OMEGA\_}
is converted to \txt{$\mathrm{\mu\Omega\_}$},
signifying micro-ohms,
and \txt{G\_OMEGA\_} is converted to \txt{$\mathrm{G\Omega\_}$},
signifying gigaohms.
Here are some other examples:

\begin{tabular}{rcl@{\hspace{5ex}}rcl}
        \txt{alpha} & \emph{becomes} & $\alpha$ &
        \txt{OMEGA13} & \emph{becomes} & $\Omega13$ \\
        \txt{alpha\_hat} & \emph{becomes} & $\alpha\_hat$ &
        \txt{theta\_elephant} & \emph{becomes} & $\theta\_elephant$ \\
        \txt{OMEGA\_} & \emph{becomes} & $\Omega\_$ &
        \txt{\_XI} & \emph{becomes} & $\_\Xi$
\end{tabular}


\subsection{Converting ASCII Symbol Sequences}
\seclabel{convert-symbol-sequences}




For the sequences of characters other than restricted words,
each is converted from left to right,
with the longest possible substring being converted at once,
with one exception:
The sequence ``\txt{(<}'' is not converted
if it is immediately followed by any of the
following characters:
`\txt{<}', '\txt{|}', `\txt{/}', `\txt{\char'134}', `\txt{*}', or `\txt{.}'.
That is, with this one exception,
the longest shorthand beginning from the first character,
if any, is converted first.
Then, the longest shorthand beginning from the next character
of the string after replacement is converted, and so on.
Here are the ASCII shorthands
for some of the characters we expect to be most frequently used:

\begin{tabular}{rcl@{\hspace{5ex}}rcl}
        \txt{[{\char'134}} & \emph{becomes} & $\bTPl$ &
        \txt{{\char'134}]} & \emph{becomes} & $\bTPr$ \\
        \txt{->}  & \emph{becomes} & $\rightarrow$ &
        \txt{=>}  & \emph{becomes} & $\Rightarrow$ \\
        \txt{$\sim$>} & \emph{becomes} & $\leadsto$ &
        \txt{|->} & \emph{becomes} & $\mapsto$ \\
        \txt{>=} & \emph{becomes} & $\geq$ &
        \txt{<=} & \emph{becomes} & $\leq$ \\
        \txt{=/=} & \emph{becomes} & $\neq$ &
        \text{...} & \emph{becomes} & $\ldots$ \\
        \txt{:=} & \emph{becomes} & $:=$ &
\end{tabular}

Although the characters with string literals
are generally not subject to this step of ASCII conversion,
They are if they are part of a restricted-word escape sequence
or a quoted-character escape sequence.
See \secref{preprocessing-string-literals} for details.

\subsection{Eliminating Ampersands}
\seclabel{convert-ampersand}

Finally,
if an ampersand is adjacent to a sequence of characters
that is changed by this step of ASCII conversion
(even if the sequence was only partly changed,
as long as the character adjacent to the ampersand is changed),
the ampersand is removed after the transformation,
\emph{unless} the ampersand is the first
or last non-whitespace character on the line.
\marginnote{Why leave the first?}
Thus, the expression
\begin{verbatim}
(GREEK_SMALL_LETTER_PHI&GREEK_SMALL_LETTER_PSI +
GREEK_SMALL_LETTER_OMEGA&GREEK_SMALL_LETTER_LAMBDA)
\end{verbatim}

is converted to:

\begin{ttt}
($\phi\psi$ +
$\omega\lambda$)

To provide a level of compatibility with Fortran,
\appref{operators} also gives short names
for the following ASCII (and thus protected) characters:

\begin{tabular}{rcl@{\hspace*{5ex}}rcl@{\hspace*{5ex}}rcl}
        \txt{LT} & \emph{becomes} & $<$ &
        \txt{GT} & \emph{becomes} & $>$ &
        \txt{EQ} & \emph{becomes} & $=$
\end{tabular}

These names are the only ones converted to a protected character.
Furthermore,
they are \emph{not} replaced by the corresponding character
unless they are delimited by whitespace characters
(\emph{not} ampersands).
Thus, they cannot participate in further conversion,
maintaining the idempotence of ASCII conversion.

# The curator's notes on the specification reader

## Decisions of his that the next run builds (2026-11-10)

- The typeset view of code and formulas is LaTeX converted to SVG, at full fidelity; the Python converter's own rendering of them goes. One SVG source serves light and dark, by a colour keyword that follows the device's setting; text in it stays selectable. The earlier process is in `explorations/fortify/` (sheets set by LaTeX and converted to SVG). Open, asked of him: whether code words inside a sentence become SVG too, or stay HTML text.
- His idea of the editions as an exhibit: the 1.0 of 2008, the working draft as the project left it, and the revival's text, with jumps between them and notes on what changed (`explorations/coordinator/HELD.md`, "Held in chat (2026-11-10)", 16:4x).

## Notes exported 2026-11-10T17:02:01Z (2 notes)

### Note 1, on the preface, the paragraph "http://projectfortress.sun.com" (`preface.html#p-0ea553b6`)

His words: "This should probably link to Wayback machine's snapshot of the page from when it existed. This is some port processing layer, which enhances the original specification text?"

The coordinator's reading: a dead link of the team's text links to the Internet Archive's snapshot from the document's own time. The source text is not changed: the converter adds the link as a layer of the edition, and marks it as the edition's addition. A Wayback address with a partial timestamp, such as `https://web.archive.org/web/2011/http://projectfortress.sun.com/`, resolves to the capture nearest that date, so no lookup is needed (the container cannot reach the Internet Archive). He asks whether this is a post-processing layer over the original text: yes, and it is to be visible as one.

### Note 2, on the preface, the paragraph "In 2026 the Fortress revival revised this working draft where a decision taken for …" (`preface.html#p-033235cb`)

His words: "You said that our additions to the specification are marked in red delete this opening. Paragraph addendum is also one such case so it should get the same treatment like distinct presentation but very very very how do you say very subtle shit some some light colored background or slight tint of course it must work in both dark and light mode and this open section should introduce this graphical element. You know like an opening of books. They're in the preamble of a book. They show how these notations are used the document so that kind of language very brief."

The coordinator's reading: the revival's paragraph in the preface is an addition of the revival like the revision callouts, so it gets the same distinct presentation; that presentation is to be very subtle, a light tint of the background, in light and in dark; and the opening of the edition introduces the graphical element in a few words, as a book's front matter explains its notation.

## His message of 2026-11-10, about 17:3x UTC, with two screenshots (the PDF's page 45 beside `lexical-structure.html` in the dark theme)

### The tables must match the PDF, and renderings are checked in a browser

His words: "When you're rendering those complex parts, you need to verify that rendering in a browser, you would have spotted that this doesn't look right, I think. And I'm now talking about the character table. I see no ampersand here. Apostrophe is indented more than the rest of the table. Like, these two screenshots don't quite match."

What the screenshots show, in chapter 4's lists "special non-operator characters" and "special operator characters":
- the `&` of U+0026 AMPERSAND is missing, and its row's second half (U+0027 APOSTROPHE) is shifted right against the rows below;
- U+27E6 and U+27E7, the white square brackets, show as `[[` and `]]`, where the PDF sets the glyphs ⟦ and ⟧;
- the `^` of U+005E shows in a code box, unlike the other characters of its column.

For the next run's worker: every table and every display is compared with the same page of the PDF (`Specification/fortress.pdf`), side by side, in a browser at a phone's and at a desktop's width, before the chapter counts as converted; a difference is fixed or listed in the README. The first run looked at parts of each chapter only.

### Inline code stays as it is

His words: "About Fortress rendering to SVG, only where it shows the render text inline in the paragraph, we should do what we've been doing." So code words and formulas inside a sentence stay HTML text, as now; examples and displays become SVG from LaTeX. This answers the question that was open above.

### The revival's callouts do not show which text changed

He first wrote that the callout's look "is fine as it is", then, reading the one in chapter 4 (see Section I.1.56): "it is like a note. I don't know which part of this is a change"; "it is basically commenting in line about the change we did, but it is not marking the text itself. It's really like our own draft notes, just not signed Victor, but by the revival. Okay. Hmm." No decision of his yet. The coordinator's proposal, put to him at 17:4x: the reader marks the changed words themselves, with a light tint, and offers the Working Draft's text of the same passage one tap away, taken from `Specification-1.0-frozen/` by comparison; the specification's own form (P-96) does not change.

### His question on section 4.17.2, a radix written as a word

"10101101_TWO is rendered as 10101101 two ... Does this spelled out radix as a word too? We don't support that, right? Does parser accept it? It didn't come up in our numeral discussion." Answered at 17:4x from the tree: the parser reads a radix as digits or as a word (`parser/Literal.rats:102-109`, `RadixNames`; `nodes_util/NodeUtil.java:1251-1280`, `radix2Number`), the team's `tests/NumeralTest.fss:18-25` asserts `f_SIXTEEN + 2` is 17 and `DEAD.BEEF_16 = DEAD.BEEF_SIXTEEN`, and the static numerals carry the radix as a number, so the spelling is gone after the parser.

### His question on the quotation marks (18:3x UTC on 2026-11-10)

He saw a backtick and a straight apostrophe in the reader where the PDF has curly single quotes, and asked whether the source holds them or the converter makes them. Found: the LaTeX source writes every single quote as a backtick and an apostrophe, and LaTeX draws the pair as curly quotes. The converter makes the same change in running text. It leaves the pair as typed where the team wrote it inside a typewriter span, as in `\txt{`FBAB'}` at `Specification/basic/lexical-structure.tex:866`, while LaTeX's typewriter font draws it curly there too. Three places in the published pages, all in the chapter on lexical structure. For the reader's next run: a quote pair that wraps the whole content of

### His rule on typography near the source (18:3x UTC on 2026-11-10)

With two screenshots of rule 2 on enclosers (the reader and the PDF), he said the reader was hard to read there and the PDF easier, and: "we should keep it as close as possible to the original source, right? We can modernize" but "we should be careful what font are we using for the source code"; the house style's code font has ligatures, which he likes for the house style, "but here we need to be careful when it renders differently in a way that it hides the ASCII part. And converts stuff to Unicode rendering when the point is to show the ASCII."

Done in `reader.css` at once, checked in a browser on that passage: code inside a sentence first lost its box and padding (the box came back, see below), so the quotation marks sit close; ligatures are off wherever code is shown; the curly quotation marks alone come from a serif face (a font face limited to U+2018 to U+201F, from fonts already on the device), since a sans face draws them like straight ticks. The three changes are the coordinator's choices under his rule. On seeing the browser picture he said of the first: "you lost The color highlight. I want that back in." So inline code keeps its highlight, with side padding cut to a tenth of an em.

# The microGPT walk-through

The pages under `docs/microgpt/` explain the flat microGPT program, `explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`, with the components that it imports and its quick check: the model and the code together, for one reader, the curator. GitHub Pages serves them at https://palimondo.github.io/fortress/microgpt/ once `main` is pushed.

## The files

- `src/NN-name.md`: the text, one file for each part. `00-index.md` is the start page's opening.
- `figs/*.svg`: the drawings, written by hand. They take their colours from the reader's stylesheet.
- `assets/walk.css`, `assets/walk.js`: what the pages add to the specification reader. The build copies them to `docs/microgpt/`.
- `build.py`: the build. It needs Python 3 with fontTools, `latex` and `dvisvgm` for the formulas and the typeset code, and `emacs`, which runs Fortify (`Fortify/fortify.el`).
- `notation.py`: the three notations of the code (below), the table of corrections to Fortify's output, and the shared fonts. `fragments.el`: the two Emacs functions that call Fortify for a file and for a list of fragments.
- `check.js`: the check in Chromium, through Playwright, at a phone's width.

`docs/microgpt/reader.css` and `reader.js` are copies of the specification reader's files in `docs/specification/`, byte for byte. The build copies them only when they are missing, or when it is run with `--reader`, so a change of the reader reaches these pages only when someone asks for it.

## Building and checking

From the repository root:

    python3 explorations/microgpt-walk/build.py --strict
    mkdir -p /tmp/walk-srv && ln -sfn "$PWD/docs" /tmp/walk-srv/fortress
    python3 -m http.server 8766 --directory /tmp/walk-srv &
    node explorations/microgpt-walk/check.js

- The build rewrites every page of `docs/microgpt/`, `tex-fonts.css` and the folder `fonts/`. It keeps the SVG files of the formulas and of the typeset code, and Fortify's LaTeX, in `tmp/microgpt-walk/`, which git ignores, and sets a formula or a line again only when its LaTeX changes. `--work DIR` names another folder for these, and `--out DIR` another folder for the pages.
- With `--strict` the build also stops on a LaTeX error in a typeset line, on a correction of the table below that applies to no line, on a character that the shared fonts lack, and on a code word that has no typeset form.
- The build reads the quoted lines from the program's files each time. It stops if a quoted fragment is not in the line that the text names. With `--strict` it also stops if some line of `MicroGptFlat.fss` is not quoted in full by the parts together; without it, it lists those lines.
- `check.js` opens every page at 390 px, light and dark, in each of the three notations. It fails on a page that scrolls sideways, on a source line that gives more than one typeset line, on a block whose line numbers or links differ between the notations, on an SVG that holds a font, on a script error and on a request that leaves the site. It checks that a first visit shows Typeset and that the choice holds from part to part and over a reload. It then writes a note, reloads, and checks the note,

# The glyphs of no width in the displays, 2026-11-16

TeX sets two glyphs of the symbol font (cmsy) with no width, so that the next sign is set over them: the slash of `\not` (code 54), which with `=` makes ≠, and the bar of `\mapsto` (code 55), which with → makes ↦. No other font that the displays use has a glyph of no width that a display uses (stmary has five, the pieces of its long arrows; no display sets one).

What each column means:

- **Slash alone.** The sign under the slash is in another font (`=` and `<` are in cmr, the slash in cmsy), or dvisvgm wrote it as a separate piece of text. The slash was then the only character of its `<text>`, a piece of text of no width. This is the kind that the curator's phone did not paint: the page showed the sign without its slash, `=` for ≠.
- **Slash beside its sign, bar of ↦.** The next sign is in the same font (∈, ≡, ⊂, →), and dvisvgm wrote the two in one `<text>`. On the phone the ↦ of section E.2.3, which is of this kind, was right. Whether every one of these was painted there is not known: no browser but Chromium runs in the container, and Chromium painted all of them.
- **Now.** All of both kinds are drawn as paths from the glyph's own outline, at the same place. In Chromium the pictures before and after are the same; `check.js` fails if a display leaves one to the text.

The lists are made from the pages as they were before the repair (commit `f766cd0d1b`), by reading each display's text: sorted by the number of lost slashes.

- **Typeset** is Fortify's rendering, the form of the specification and of the team's papers. Fortify sets each of the program's files whole, one output line for each source line, and each fragment alone. A quoted line becomes one SVG, set by `latex` and converted by `dvisvgm`, drawn in `currentColor` with its text as text, so one file serves light and dark. A code word in a sentence becomes HTML text in the reader's classes for a formula in a sentence (`notation.tex_html`), with the inline highlight of a code word.
- **Unicode** is the source after the specification's ASCII conversion (Appendix "ASCII to Unicode" and `operators.tex`), outside strings and comments: the brackets `[\ \]`, the arrows and comparisons, the operators' short names and the Greek letters' short names. The table in `notation.py` is written by hand for the tokens of this program. `ZZ32` and `RR64` stay as typed: the double-struck letter is a rule of rendering (Appendix "Rendering of Fortress Identifiers", rule (a)), not a character of the source. `SUM` becomes ∑, as the specification converts it, though today's parser does not yet take the sign as a big operator (the gap ledger's row 5).
- **ASCII** is the source as it is in the files.

"""## The glyphs of no width

The curator's note of 2026-11-16: on his phone the table of section E.2.3 of Appendix E showed `=` in the row "`=/=` becomes ≠", where the PDF shows ≠ (`curator-notes.md`).

- **The cause.** TeX has no glyph for ≠. It sets the slash of `\\not` (code 54 of the symbol font cmsy), a glyph whose width is zero and whose ink lies to the right of its place, and then `=` over it. The bar of `\\mapsto` (code 55) is the same kind, set before →. dvisvgm writes each as a character whose advance is zero. The slash and `=` are in different fonts (cmsy and cmr), so the slash came out alone: `<text class='t2' x='80.33' y='56.19'></text>`, a piece of text of no width. Nothing was lost in the conversion: the LaTeX, the DVI, the SVG and the font piece all held the slash, and Chromium painted it. The phone's browser did not paint that piece of text. The bar of ↦, which stands in one `<text>` with its arrow, was painted there.
- **Not shown here.** No browser but Chromium runs in the container (Playwright's WebKit lacks its system libraries), so the phone's picture was not reproduced, and which rule of its browser drops the piece is not established; the reading above rests on his report, on the SVG, and on the difference between the slash (alone, lost) and the bar (with its arrow, kept).
- **The repair** (`draw_widthless` in `spec2html.py`). After the fonts are read, every character whose glyph has an advance of zero is taken out of the text of every display, and the glyph's outline, read from the same font piece, is drawn at its place as `<path class='nw'>`. Nothing else moves, since the glyph had no advance. This covers the slash alone, the slash beside its sign and the bar: 161 glyphs in the Working Draft and 177 in the revised edition, on 20 pages of each. The build fails if a display still leaves such a glyph to the text. In Chromium the displays look as before.
- **The places.** `widthless-glyphs-2026-11-16.md` lists them by page and section. The lost kind, the slash alone, stood at 68 places of the Working Draft and 84 of the revised edition, each showing its sign without the slash (`=` for ≠ at 45 and 55 of them). The worst: section 33.1, Rational Numbers (25 in the Working Draft); sections I.1.11 to I.1.13 and I.1.25 of Appendix I in the revised edition (42); section 41.1 (9 in each); the rules of the calculi in sections A.2.2, A.3.3 and A.4.3 (12 in each), where a premise read `=` for ≠.
- **Inside a sentence** a formula is HTML text, and the converter writes ≠, ∉ and their like as one Unicode character, so nothing of this kind is there. Where Unicode has no character for a negated sign, the converter writes the sign and U+0338, the combining slash, which the device's font draws: 24 places in each edition, most in chapter 34 (⊏, ⊐, ⊒, ≣ and others). They were not changed. input.message:
**Cause.** TeX has no glyph for ≠: it sets the slash of `\not`, a glyph of width zero, and `=` over it; the conversion lost nothing (LaTeX, DVI, SVG and the font piece all hold the slash, and Chromium paints it), but the slash came out alone in its `<text>`, a piece of text of no width, which the phone's browser did not paint. This last step is inferred, not shown: only Chromium runs in the container (Playwright's WebKit lacks system libraries), and the inference rests on his report plus the fact that the bar of ↦, which shares a `<text>` with its arrow, was painted. So the answer to his question is no: no script of conversions makes that table.
**Repair** (`spec2html.py`, `draw_widthless`): every glyph of advance zero is taken out of a display's text and drawn as a path from its own outline in the same font; the build fails if one is left. Chromium's picture of E.2.3 is the same before and after; the phone still has to confirm it.
**Other places**: 161 glyphs in the Working Draft and 177 in the revised edition, on 20 pages each. The lost kind (slash alone) is 68 and 84 of them, with `=` for ≠ at 45 and 55. Worst: section 33.1 Rational Numbers (25, Working Draft); sections I.1.11–13 and I.1.25 of Appendix I (42, revised); the calculi's rules A.2.2, A.3.3, A.4.3 (12 each, a premise read `=` for ≠); then 41.1 (9 each). The rest are 37 slashes beside their sign and 56 bars of ↦, now drawn too. Full list by page and section: `/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/spec-html/widthless-glyphs-2026-11-16.md`.
**Found beside it and repaired**: inside a sentence, `S \not\excludes D` showed the word "mathrel" with a slash; it now shows ◊ with the slash. 25 other inline negations per edition use the combining U+0338 and were left alone.
**Why `compare.js` missed it**: it looks through Chromium, which painted the slash, and it measures the share of a whole display's ink. A trial that hid the glyphs showed a lost slash is a 12–24 pixel piece, while sound displays differ by pieces up to 33, so no limit separates them; `compare.js` is unchanged. `check.js` now fails on any visible character of extent zero in a display: it passes on both editions (46 and 43 checks) and fails on the pages as they were.
**Other checks, both editions**: `compare.js` 1,177 displays / 3 differ and 1,229 / 4 differ, the same displays as on 2026-11-15; `pdfcheck.py` 17 and 7 blocks not found, one fewer each.
**Note ids**: the glyph repair moved none. The `\not\excludes` repair moved one paragraph: `overloaded-functional.html#p-e3f30724` → `#p-c3996be5` (Working Draft) and `revival/spec-changes.html#p-f691a211` → `#p-69abb85a` (revised); none of his notes is on it.
**Walk-through table**: new `explorations/microgpt-walk/check_unicode_table.py` checked 67 entries; one was wrong: `CROSS` gave × (U+00D7) where the operator tables give ⨯ (U+2A2F), now corrected. None is missing from the appendix; `ZZ32` and `RR64` untouched. The program does not use `CROSS`, so the rebuild of `docs/microgpt/` changed no page.
**Not done**: the walk-through's `check.js` was not rerun, since its pages are unchanged. Both rebuilds rewrote the `.woff2` pieces with different bytes for the same fonts; I restored the committed ones rather than commit that churn. `curator-notes.md` and both READMEs are brought in line.
**Commits**, all pushed to the three refs: `2efd6e4d22`, `3ae5596f73`, `6ff21149df`, `aeb01a0954`.
